newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Marchers in Central African Republic back mutineers.
newsitem.headline: Marchers in Central African Republic back mutineers.

text.p: Over 300 marchers supporting army mutineers in the Central African Republic capital Bangui, some carrying bodies, on Wednesday accused France of backing African peacekeepers trying to crush them, witnesses said.

The demonstrators, who marched peacefully to the French embassy, accused the former colonial power and the peacekeepers of siding with President Ange-Felix Patasse after five days of clashes in which at least 58 people have died.

Occasional small-arms fire crackled through the night, but it was quieter than on Tuesday when peacekeepers used heavy weapons to crush disaffected soldiers, some of whom had not responded to a January peace deal to return to their units.

The local Red Cross said it had been swamped by the arrival of tens of thousands of people who fled the southern districts loyal to mutineers, which the peacekeepers bombarded with shells from tanks and heavy mortars.

"There is not enough drinking water, there is not enough food," Dr David Dofara, head of the local Red Cross, told Reuters. He said the number of people displaced by fighting increased to over 40,000 on Wednesday from around 8,000 before.

A spokesman for the African force, sent to bring peace after a string of mutinies between pro- and anti-Patasse factions in the army, said the force had handed 85 mutineers captured in fighting to the Presidential Guard.
Captain Lamine Gueye told Reuters it was not the job of the peacekeepers to "act as police".
The death toll on Tuesday was at least 58 based on a Red Cross body count, while witnesses, whose stories tallied, gave a figure of at least 104 dead, according to Dofara.

There was no sign in the frightened city of Mali's widely respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, who brokered the January 25 agreement, and who on Monday said he was returning to Bangui.

The peace deal the African force came to implement was preceded by three mutinies in less than a year in which political and ethnic supporters of Patasse in the army clashed with former comrades who became bitter enemies.

French troops are stationed in Bangui under a defence accord, but the former colonial power, which last year intervened to stop clashes, denied on Tuesday they were directly helping the African force.

After the latest fighting, Bangui's African force is looking less like a realistic model for bringing peace to Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Congo -- where it has been touted as a possible solution after over two weeks of sporadic clashes.

Mutinies in April and May 1996 in Bangui began as protests over pay but evolved into a movement to topple Patasse, a civilian from the north of the country elected in 1993. The third mutiny began in November and degenerated into ethnic bloodshed.
Most of the mutineers are members of the Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The 800-strong African force includes soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. A Senegalese soldier killed on Friday was among the first casualties of the flare-up.
